record.label: Strict curvature on a positive constant interval
record.statement: For every gamma in U and its controlled diffusion, if gamma=c>0 on an open interval I contained in (0,1), then q'''(t)>=(1/(1000*c^2))E[(cPhi_xx(t,X_t))^4]>0 for every t in I. Hence q' is strictly convex on I. The same local assertion applies to each interior point of (a,b) with 0<=a<b<1; the endpoints are reached by continuity of q'.
record.boundary: Curated source-level mathematical statement, not an elaborated Lean extraction or independently accepted proof. Its displayed local hypotheses are quantified guards; a hypothetical plateau is not an added premise of the full-support theorem. Unconditional with respect to minimization; conditional on admissibility and a positive plateau. The cited Lean positive_gap_curvature supplies the positivity of the second derivative of curvatureMoment, not a claim of literal equality between every manuscript lemma and a Lean type.

aligned_passages.text: ### 2.1 Structure of the argument The proof begins with regularity on strips bounded away from terminal time. It makes the diffusion $X$ and the gradient moment $q$ available, so a first variation can show where the minimizer is in contact. On a constant interval, the shape inequalities and the rational certificate give the strict curvature needed to contradict that contact. The zero-interval case uses a separate heat argument, and the possible terminal plateau needs its own exclusion. These steps lead to full support and the two moment equalities. In this manuscript route, the value argument then uses bounded-martingale convergence and the attained Parisi formula to express $P_*$ as a terminal Brownian correlation and an integral of expected curvature. Section 6 defines the terminal martingale variable and proves these equalities. The fixed-$T$ Gaussian approximation recovers this integral through Euler coupling, orthogonal normalization and mean-preserving rounding. The QAOA theorem additionally requires rooted energy identification, classical synthesis, removal of temporary seeds and transfer to fixed angles. The main route is §§3–5, then §§6–7, then §§8.1–8.6; §12 compares the two formal interfaces. The original analytic details are in [OpenAI (2026a), §§2–7][fs-main], and the circuit construction is in [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–6][q-intro]. The density theorem in §§9.1–9.2 is a further consequence of support and the PDE, not a premise of the scalar or circuit construction. The positive-temperature route in §11.1 independently supplies the same bounded classical input used for synthesis. The probability consequence in §11.2 requires a separate fixed-word second-moment theorem. These branches explain why the two selected formal statements are not a formal proof of the complete circuit theorem. These destinations separate premises of the support proof from its consequences. They locate the detailed arguments behind the short paper's support and density theorem. **The diffusion and moment identity.** For any admissible $\gamma$, the compact-strip estimates justify defining $X,q$ and computing $q'=\mathbb E a^2$; see [§2.4](#strip-estimates) and [§3.1](#gradient-moment). **Variational contact.** Minimality, admissible mass addition and compact mass removal give $G\ge0$, its vanishing on support and the contact slopes. The steps are in [§3.2](#feasible-variation), [§3.3](#measure-contact) and [§3.4](#contact-slopes). **Strict curvature.** Admissibility and a positive constant $c$ on an interval suffice; minimality is not needed. The shape comparisons, algebra and limiting argument are in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons), [§4.4](#curvature-algebra) and [§4.5](#plateau-limit). **Exclusion of gaps.** Combine contact with the appropriate positive, zero or terminal argument. The cases have separate destinations: [terminal](#terminal-gap), [bounded](#bounded-gaps) and [initial](#initial-gaps) gaps. **Positive density.** Full support comes first. Differentiated moments then give [smoothness in §9.1](#smooth-density-consequence), and a local comparison gives [strict positivity in §9.2](#positive-density). **Value and circuits.** Retain the same minimizer and diffusion through [the value identity in §6](#scalar-value-identities) and [the finite Gaussian construction in §7](#finite-gaussian-approximation). [The circuit argument in §8](#qaoa-construction) requires additional theorems. ### 2.2 The regularity available before the proof starts **Proposition 2.1 (compact-strip regularity).** For $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ and $0\le T<1$, the value has bounded, jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every positive finite order on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$. If admissible coefficients converge in $L^1$ and their smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz terminal values converge uniformly to $|x|$, these spatial derivatives converge uniformly on each such strip. The bounds depend on the derivative order, the fixed strip and a common coefficient mass bound. Time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere across coefficient jumps. On an open constant interval, the heat formula supplies the additional time smoothness used in §4. The terminal estimate is $$ |x|\le\Phi_\gamma(t,x) \le |x|+\sqrt{2(1-t)/\pi}+\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds. $$ It controls approach to $|x|$ without differentiating that cusp. The strip estimates justify the interior calculations and finite meshes; the terminal bound and integrability justify the later endpoint limits. The two roles must remain separate. Their uses depend on the region and limit. On a fixed $[0,T]$ with $T<1$, bounded spatial derivatives and locally absolutely continuous time dependence justify the Itô identities and Euler coupling. Across a jump of $\gamma$, the spatial derivative moments remain continuous and the time equations hold almost everywhere; this is enough for contact slopes and the endpoint chord comparison. Inside a constant interval, classical time differentiation permits the strict-curvature calculation. As $T\uparrow1$, the controls change: the displayed value bound, integrable coefficient tails and martingale convergence justify first variation and terminal value. No differentiated estimate at the terminal cusp is used. These are [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1 and its diffusion consequences][fs-reg]; [§2.4](#strip-estimates) reconstructs their uniformity. The hypotheses also have distinct uses. Zero field supplies evenness, $u(0,0)=0$ and reflection in the shape argument. The convention $\xi''=1$ fixes the curvature coefficients. Monotonicity gives bounded coefficients before time one and nonnegative coefficient jumps; it also turns a support gap into a constant interval. Integrability controls terminal tails and Fubini interchanges, while local finiteness of the Stieltjes measure is enough for compact mass removal. Minimality first enters through the variational inequality in §3; the constant-interval curvature estimate itself applies to an admissible coefficient without assuming it is a minimiser. [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]; [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), §6][fs-var]. ### 2.3 Which prior results play which role The imported ground-state formula supplies two facts with different uses. Auffinger and Chen's Theorem 1 identifies the ground-state limit with an infimum over $\mathcal U$. To choose a coefficient attaining that infimum, one must also use their construction in the proof of Lemma 3. In the cited arXiv v2, the theorem is on p. 3, the compactness construction is on pp. 7–9, and the lower-bound proof is on pp. 11–12. Here is the part of that construction which supplies the witness. Let $\alpha_\beta$ be a positive-temperature Parisi distribution function. The source bounds $\beta\alpha_\beta(t)$ uniformly on each interval ending before one. Helly selection and a diagonal subsequence produce a nonnegative, nondecreasing right-continuous limit $\gamma_0$. In the SK normalization, the source's weighted integral bound also controls $\int_0^1\beta\alpha_\beta(t)\,dt$. For every nonnegative nondecreasing $h$, splitting at $1/2$ gives $\int_0^1 h(t)\,dt\le4\int_0^1t h(t)\,dt$: the first half is bounded by $h(1/2)/2$, and on the second half $t\ge1/2$. Fatou's lemma then gives $\gamma_0\in\mathcal U$. Mass can concentrate at time one during this limit, so compact convergence alone does not identify the limiting control problem. Write the limiting measure of the time coefficients as $$ \nu_0(dt)=\gamma_0(t)\,dt+m\delta_1(dt),\qquad m\geq0. $$ For an arbitrary admissible control, let $S$ denote its terminal state with coefficient $\gamma_0$. To see why the terminal choice is admissible, let the original control be $\alpha$ and put $S_s=B_s+\int_0^s\gamma_0(r)\alpha_r\,dr$. For a cutoff $\tau<1$ use $\alpha_s$ before $\tau$ and $g_k(S_s)$ afterwards, where $g_k$ is a continuous function bounded by one and converging pointwise to the sign with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=1$. This control uses only information available at time $s$. At fixed $\tau,k$, first take the temperature limit; then let $\tau\uparrow1$ and $k\to\infty$. The continuous terminal evaluation has thereby approached $\operatorname{sgn}(S)$ without anticipating a future state. The endpoint atom then contributes $$ |S+m\operatorname{sgn}(S)|-|S|=m $$ to the reward and $$ \tfrac12m\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(S)^2+1\bigr)=m $$ to the combined control and Parisi penalties. These contributions cancel. Taking the supremum over the remaining controls proves $P_*\geq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)$. The upper bound proved earlier in that paper gives $P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$. Therefore $$ P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma) \leq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)\leq P_*. $$ Thus $\gamma_0$ attains the infimum. The cancellation is a step in the imported existence proof; it is not an additional assumption about the Stieltjes measure $d\gamma_0$. In particular, $\nu_0$ here is the limit of coefficient-times-Lebesgue measures, not the order parameter's Stieltjes measure. The two measures must not be identified. [Auffinger and Chen, arXiv:1606.05335v2, pp. 7–12][ac17]. The cited theorem is stated for the almost-sure normalized maximum. Its expected-value formulation used here follows from Gaussian concentration. For $L_n=n^{-1}\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma)$, the Lipschitz constant in the Gaussian couplings is $\sqrt{(n-1)/(2n^2)}$. Hence $L_n-\mathbb E L_n\to0$ in probability. Since the almost-sure limit is the deterministic Parisi value, the deterministic sequence $\mathbb E L_n$ has the same limit. The full-support theorem below remains conditional on a minimizer; neither of the selected formal interfaces constructs one. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, Introduction, ground-state formula and its footnote][fs-main]. Auffinger–Chen–Zeng's infinite support does not exclude an interior gap. Their terminal-plateau observation anticipates one endpoint obstruction; the argument below supplies the quantitative boundary-layer proof used here. The full-support manuscript develops a rational coercivity route and credits Chen's 2026 theorem for the same full-support conclusion and smooth absolute continuity. Chen's Proposition 4.2 has the conditional crossing form $q''(t)=0\Rightarrow q'''(t)>0$; the cited rational certificate gives $q'''(t)>0$ throughout a positive constant interval. These are different sufficient mechanisms, and this record makes no priority claim for full support. [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1 and Remark 7][acz]; [Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 4.2][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The transformed density comparisons also have antecedents in Lopatto's positive-temperature analysis and Chen's zero-temperature analysis; the rational coercive identity is the different step in the full-support proof. Zhou's positive-temperature interval-support result applies near the critical temperature, whereas Lopatto's cited theorem covers the low-temperature zero-field phase. Neither transfers full Stieltjes support to zero temperature on its own: for the minimizers, $\beta\mu_\beta$ converges vaguely on $[0,1)$ to the zero-temperature Stieltjes measure, while the unscaled Parisi probability measures converge weakly on $[0,1]$ to $\delta_1$. These are different measures and topologies. Convergence without an interval-specific lower bound can lose support information. The direct zero-temperature gap proof below is therefore essential. [Chen (2026), Remarks 1.4–1.5][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. Two later editions sharpen the comparison without entering the pinned September proof. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, Proposition 5.1 and (5.8)–Corollary 5.6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4), proves a conditional curvature crossing on a positive constant interval. Its integrating factor makes a transformed curvature derivative strictly increasing, so the associated contact derivative decreases and then increases; it does not assert an unconditional positive third derivative. [Lopatto, arXiv:2610.00127v1, Theorem 2.3 and §8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00127v1), works at positive temperature and positive external field. Its comparison requires one-sided bounds on the coefficient before and after the chosen time, a moment inequality and a stationarity equality. The subsequent moment bootstrap yields smooth, strictly positive density on a nontrivial support interval; a singleton support is a separate case. Neither theorem removes the hypotheses of the zero-temperature argument below. Here is an explicit example of the information lost in such a limit. It concerns admissible measures, not Parisi minimizers. Put $g=\mathbf1_{[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1)}$ and $q_n=1-n^{-2}$, and for $n\ge2$ define $$ \mu_n(dt)=\frac{g(t)+n^{-1}}n\mathbf1_{[0,q_n]}(t)\,dt +\left(1-\frac1n\int_0^{q_n}(g(t)+n^{-1})\,dt\right)\delta_{q_n}(dt). $$ The continuous part has mass at most $(2/3+1/n)/n<1$, so these are probability measures with a positive endpoint atom. Their density is positive throughout $[0,q_n]$, giving $\operatorname{supp}\mu_n=[0,q_n]$. Their continuous mass tends to zero and $q_n\to1$, hence $\mu_n\Rightarrow\delta_1$ weakly on $[0,1]$. For a compactly supported continuous test function on $[0,1)$, the endpoint atom eventually lies outside its support. Consequently $n\mu_n\to g(t)\,dt$ vaguely there, although the limit vanishes on $(1/3,2/3)$. Even the cumulative coefficients converge in the topology used for the PDE: with $\gamma_n(t)=n\mu_n([0,t])$ and $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$, their difference is $t/n$ below $q_n$, and $\gamma_n=n$ on the terminal strip of length $n^{-2}$. Thus $$ \|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}\le\frac1{2n}+\frac1n\longrightarrow0. $$ Every $\gamma_n$ is admissible, but $d\gamma$ has an interior gap. Minimality and the gap argument supply information that these convergences alone do not. An atom added at time one is likewise invisible to the coefficient on $[0,1)$ and hence to its PDE and variational functional; the zero-temperature problem does not select an endpoint mass. Control and gradient-martingale methods have antecedents in [Auffinger–Chen](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-014-2254-z) and [Jagannath–Tobasco](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04398v4). A finite-temperature theorem with smooth terminal value $\log\cosh$ does not alone establish the result with terminal cusp $|x|$. The required compact-strip and terminal estimates are supplied in [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [Chen–Handschy–Lerman](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4) supplies earlier zero-temperature regularity, control and uniqueness results (Theorem 4 for uniqueness). This is distinct from the earlier finite-temperature uniqueness result of Auffinger and Chen. [Montanari](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10897v2) and [El Alaoui–Montanari–Sellke](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00904v1) inform normalised discretisation and optimisation. ### 4.5 A fixed-time inequality and its plateau application **Proposition 4.1 (coercivity at a fixed time).** Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ and let $X$ be its associated diffusion, started at zero. Suppose that $00$. With $a=\Phi_{xx}$, $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$, evaluated at $(t,X_t)$, one has $$ \mathcal C_\gamma(t):=\mathbb E[d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4] \ge \frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E a^4. \tag{4.1} $$ Neither minimality nor a constant neighbourhood of $t$ is assumed. This is the common estimate behind plateau curvature and positive density. When $\gamma$ is smooth near $t$, Itô's formula gives $q''=\mathbb E b^2-2\gamma\mathbb E a^3$ and $$ (\mathbb E b^2)'=\mathbb E d^2-6\gamma\mathbb E(ab^2),\qquad (\mathbb E a^3)'=3\mathbb E(ab^2)-3\gamma\mathbb E a^4. $$ Differentiating the first identity therefore gives $$ q'''(t)+2\gamma'(t)\mathbb E a^3=\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \tag{4.2} $$ On a plateau the coefficient derivative vanishes. At a smooth minimizer, $q=t$ makes the third derivative of $q$ vanish instead. **Proof.** Fix $t **The spatial inequality at a coefficient jump.** Continuity at $t$ is a sufficient hypothesis in Proposition 4.1 and in the retained sampled formal interface. The ordinary spatial-moment argument permits a little more. Fix $c=\gamma(t)>0$ and replace $\gamma$ by $c$ on $[t-\delta,t+\delta)$, leaving it unchanged elsewhere. Monotonicity preserves both joins and right continuity. For fixed $0<\delta_0<\min(t,1-t)$ and $0<\delta\le\delta_0$, $$ \|\gamma_\delta-\gamma\|_1 \le2\delta\,\gamma(t+\delta_0)\longrightarrow0. $$ Thus local boundedness suffices for the same strip stability and coupled expectation limit. Each replacement has a positive plateau at $t$, so (4.1) holds at a jump too, with the stated right-continuous value $c$. This extension concerns spatial moments only: it supplies no time derivative $q'''(t)$ or $\gamma'(t)$ at a jump and does not remove a hypothesis from the retained Lean declaration. Neither application below requires this extension. **Corollary 4.2 (positive plateaus).** Suppose now that $\gamma=c>0$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$ and $t\in I$. Then (4.2) gives $q'''(t)=\mathcal C_\gamma(t)$. To establish strictness for this limiting solution, choose $b\in I$ later than $t$ and put $\psi=\Phi_\gamma(b,\cdot)$. This is smooth, convex, even and a bounded distance from $|x|$, so $\psi'$ cannot be constant. The Cole–Hopf formula gives $$ \Phi_{xx}(t,x) =\mathbb E^{\rm tilt}_{t,x}\psi'' +c\operatorname{Var}^{\rm tilt}_{t,x}(\psi'), $$ $$ \nu_{t,x}(dy)= \frac{e^{c\psi(y)}p_{b-t}(y-x)} {\int_{\mathbb R}e^{c\psi(z)}p_{b-t}(z-x)\,dz}\,dy. $$ The tilted density is positive everywhere. Its variance of the nonconstant continuous function $\psi'$ is strictly positive; its mean of $\psi''$ is nonnegative. Thus $v(t,x)>0$ for every $x$, and $\mathbb E v(t,X_t)^4>0$. Combining the limiting inequality with the differentiated identity proves $q'''(t)\ge(1000c^2)^{-1}\mathbb E v(t,X_t)^4>0$. This proves strict convexity of $q'$ on $I$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][fs-reg]; [Proposition 5.1][fs-curv]. ### 4.6 Why the zero interval remains a separate case When $c=0$, the heat equation gives $q''(t)=\mathbb E\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2$ without division by $c$. Start the drift-free evolution at an earlier point of $I$; its Gaussian transition kernel makes the law of $X_t$ have a positive density everywhere. If the expectation were zero, continuity would force $\Phi_{xxx}(t,\cdot)\equiv0$. Then $\Phi(t,\cdot)$ would be an even quadratic polynomial. Its one-Lipschitz bound forces that polynomial to be constant, contradicting its bounded distance from $|x|$. Therefore $q''(t)>0$, giving strict increase of $q'$. **Lemma 2 (constant-interval curvature; [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][FS]).** Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$, with its associated diffusion and moment $q$. If $\gamma=c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, called a plateau, then for $t\in I$ $$ q'''(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0 \quad\text{if }c>0. \tag{3} $$ If $c=0$, then $q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0$. Minimality is not a hypothesis of this lemma. Section 3 derives its moment polynomial and explains the integrated estimate imported from the source. **Proof of Theorem 1, assuming Lemma 2.** A complementary interval with two support endpoints admits two contact conditions; an initial interval without support at zero has coefficient zero; a terminal interval is handled here by a boundary estimate. Suppose $(\ell,r)$ is a support gap with endpoints in $S$ and $r<1$. The coefficient is a positive constant there: support at $\ell$ and absence of mass immediately to its right force $\mu_\gamma([0,\ell])>0$. Strict convexity of $q'$ and (2) give $$ q'(t)<\frac{r-t}{r-\ell}q'(\ell) +\frac{t-\ell}{r-\ell}q'(r)\leq1 \qquad(\ell0$, hence $q'(t)0$ and all $t$ sufficiently close to one. Two estimates produce this scale. The heat representation of the terminal value $|x|$ gives $1-u(t,x)^2\geq\kappa>0$ on $|x|\leq\sqrt{1-t}$. A transition-kernel comparison from a fixed earlier time gives a density $f_t(x)\geq m>0$ on the fixed window $|x|\leq1$, uniformly as $t\uparrow1$. Thus $$ 1-q(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}(1-u(t,x)^2)f_t(x)\,dx \geq2m\kappa\sqrt{1-t}. $$ The time-uniform density estimate, proved in Lemma 6.3, equations (6.6)–(6.7), is essential; pointwise positivity of each density would not suffice. For $h=1-t[long §5, “A shorter qualitative exclusion”](../long/reasoning-record.md#qualitative-terminal-gap). The boundary estimate retained here also describes the terminal behaviour of an arbitrary coefficient constant near one. The zero-coefficient heat argument and late-step variation have antecedents in [Chen, Handschy and Lerman (2018), Theorem 6 and its proof][CHL]. These cases exhaust the complement of the relatively closed set $S$. Consequently $S=[0,1)$, contact gives $q(t)=t$, and differentiation gives $\mathbb E a^2=1$, including the right-hand value at zero. Moreover, $\gamma(t_2)-\gamma(t_1)=\mu_\gamma((t_1,t_2])>0$. This proves Theorem 1 using the stated analytic inputs.

The quantity used in both arguments is a spatial moment. Write $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$, and, for $00$. For its associated diffusion, $$ \mathcal C_\gamma(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000} \mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ Neither minimality nor a constant neighbourhood of $t$ is required. This is the consequence of [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1 and Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS] stated in the companion's [Proposition 4.1, §4.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-time-coercivity). We first explain the positive-plateau estimate, then obtain this fixed-time form by inserting a short plateau. For a smooth coefficient the identity connecting the two applications is $$ q'''+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3=\mathcal C_\gamma. $$ On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$; at a smooth minimiser, full support gives $q=t$ and hence $q'''=0$. Section 4 proves the required smoothness before using the second identity. On a plateau with $\gamma=c>0$, put $r=c\Phi_x=c u$, $v=r_x=c a$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. This rescaling makes the derivative identities polynomial. The PDE becomes $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$, and the diffusion has spatial generator $\tfrac12\partial_{xx}+r\partial_x$. Differentiating in space and applying Itô's formula gives the drift and diffusion pairs $(0,v)$, $(-v^2,w)$ and $(-3vw,z)$ for $r,v,w$, respectively. All expectations in this section evaluate spatial functions at $(t,X_t)$. Starting with $c^2q'=\mathbb E v^2$, Itô's formula gives $$ \begin{aligned} c^2q''&=\mathbb E[w^2-2v^3],\\ c^2q'''&=\mathbb E[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4] =c^2\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \end{aligned} \tag{4} $$ For example, the drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$, respectively. The negative mixed term is the obstacle. Convexity, which gives $v\geq0$, does not control it. Indeed, for the smooth auxiliary terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$ and coefficient $\gamma\equiv1$, the solution is $\Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+(1-t)/2$. Thus $r=\tanh x$; at $r^2=1/2$, the polynomial in (4) equals $-19/8$. This is a finite-step smoothing example, not a minimiser of the absolute-value-terminal problem; its calculation is given in [long §4.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-moments). The proof subtracts a spatial derivative whose expectation under the law of $X_t$ is zero. The resulting expression has a positive fourth-moment remainder. The backward value function and the forward density must satisfy joint shape restrictions for this decomposition to have the required signs. Those comparisons and the exact polynomial identity are the substantial inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), §§3–4][FS]. We explain their roles first for finite-step coefficients, then pass the integrated inequality to an integrable coefficient by approximation. Begin with a positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficient $\gamma_{\rm step}$: a function constant on each interval of a finite partition. Replace the terminal value $|x|$ by the smooth approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$, with $M\geq\|\gamma_{\rm step}\|_\infty$. On a step of height $c$, set $h=e^{c\Phi}$. Then $h_t=-h_{xx}/2$ and $r=h_x/h$. The same exponential removes the drift from the forward density equation. Indeed, writing $f=hg$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} f_t&=\tfrac12(hg)_{xx}-(h_xg)_x\\ &=-\tfrac12h_{xx}g+\tfrac12hg_{xx} =h_tg+\tfrac12hg_{xx}. \end{aligned} $$ Comparison with $f_t=h_tg+hg_t$ yields $g_t=g_{xx}/2$. Thus one backward heat factor and one forward heat factor determine the law against which the moment polynomial is integrated. For $s=-\partial_x\log g$, the source proves joint shape restrictions: on $x>0$, $r_x>0$ and $s_x\geq1/t$, both $r$ and $s$ are concave, and $H:=w/(2r)+v\leq0$ is nondecreasing. They also give $$ j:=s_x-(s/r)v=r\,\partial_x(s/r)\geq0. $$ The last inequality couples the backward gradient to the forward density; separate monotonicity and concavity do not supply it. On the first step, $s=x/t$, so concavity of $r$ gives $j\geq0$. A parabolic comparison propagates the sign within each step. At a forward jump with $k=c_+/c_-\geq1$, continuity of $\Phi$ and $f$ gives $$ r_+=kr_-,\qquad s_+=s_-+(k-1)r_-,\qquad j_+=(s_x)_+-\frac{s_+}{r_+}(r_x)_+=j_-. $$ The joint sign therefore survives coefficient jumps as well. The quotients $w/r$ and $s/r$ extend smoothly through zero because $r,s,w$ are odd and $r_x(0)>0$. The comparison's boundary controls and these extensions are analytic inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 3.2–3.4][FS], reconstructed in [long §4.3](../long/reasoning-record.md#shape-comparisons). The factorisation of the density gives $f_x/f=r-s$. For a suitable expression $F$ in the shape quantities, define $$ \mathcal W(F)=r\partial_xF+(v+r^2-rs)F. $$ Then $f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF)$. The smooth extensions avoid an interior boundary term at zero, and the source's differentiated Gaussian tail estimates give $rfF\to0$ at both spatial infinities for the polynomial correction used below. Hence $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$, where $\mathbb E_f$ denotes integration against $f(x)\,dx$. The remaining step is algebra under these analytic restrictions. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 4.1][FS] supplies an explicit polynomial $F_2$ and a decomposition $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4 =\mathcal W(F_2)+\kappa v^4+\mathcal R, \qquad \mathcal R\geq0,\qquad \kappa=\frac{1661507}{1521000000}>\frac1{1000}. $$ The coefficients of $F_2$ have both signs; no sign of $F_2$ or $\mathcal W(F_2)$ is needed, since the correction integrates to zero. In contrast, the shape inequalities make every term of $\mathcal R$ nonnegative. Two of its actual terms are $$ \frac{337}{10000}\,r^2j\,(-w/r-7v)^2, \qquad (2rH_x)v\left(\frac{2331}{10000}r^2+\frac{87}{2500}j\right). $$ The first needs the joint comparison $j\geq0$; the second also uses $H_x\geq0$ on the positive half-line. Reflection preserves these signs on the negative half-line. The remaining terms use $H\leq0$, forward concavity and the other shape bounds. Thus the decomposition is positive on the shapes supplied by the PDE, not on arbitrary spatial derivatives. Integration removes $\mathcal W(F_2)$ and keeps the fourth-moment margin, giving $$ \int_{\mathbb R}(z^2-12vw^2+6v^4)f\,dx \geq\frac1{1000}\int_{\mathbb R}v^4f\,dx. \tag{5} $$ We use (5) as an imported analytic estimate. The full polynomial and its decomposition are in [Lemma 4.1 and Table 1][certificate]; Proposition 4.2 integrates them using the signs and zero boundary flux supplied by Lemma 3.4. [Long §4.4, “How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful”](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-algebra) reproduces the definitions and complete identity. Spatial derivatives through order four converge uniformly on a fixed strip below one, and the diffusions driven by the same Brownian motion converge (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 2.1–2.2 and Proposition 5.1][FS]). Only $v,w,z$ remain in (5), so no convergence theorem for the auxiliary logarithmic derivative $s$ is needed. Dividing by $c^2$ gives (3); strictness follows from $\Phi_{xx}>0$ on the plateau (see [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][FS]). For $0<\delta<\min(t,1-t)$ define $$ \gamma_\delta(s)= \begin{cases} c,&t-\delta\leq s0$, then $q'$ cannot attain an interior maximum. The endpoint slope bounds therefore give $q'<1$ inside the gap and the same strict area deficit. Bare strict positivity could be lost in that limit.

Adding a small atom at scale $s$ raises the cumulative function at
*every* later scale. It is always allowed: the total mass is not
fixed, so no compensating removal is required. Its direction is
$\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$, equal to zero before $s$ and one
from $s$ onward. Thus

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]
=\frac12\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt=:\frac12G(s).
$$

For the candidate in Figure 1, adding $\varepsilon$ mass at $s=1/2$
creates a jump of height $\varepsilon$ there and raises the entire
remaining curve by $\varepsilon$. The coefficient changes only on
that tail, but its optimised value and feedback must be recomputed:
earlier starting states also face a changed future control problem. The
first-variation theorem accounts for this dependence. Its formula
has a tail integral because that is where the coefficient changes:
$G(s)/2$ is the marginal cost of placing mass at $s$. At a minimiser,
$G(s)\ge0$ for every $s<1$.

For the two weights in Section 2, the same accounting gives

$$
\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=2G(1/4)+G(3/4).
$$

Each weight is charged for its entire remaining tail. The $q$ and $G$
in this identity belong to that candidate; no optimality has been assumed.
Reducing both weights by a fraction $\varepsilon$ multiplies the
cumulative function by $1-\varepsilon$.

Suppose temporarily that this two-weight candidate minimised
$\mathcal P$. Addition would give two nonnegative costs,
$G(1/4)\ge0$ and $G(3/4)\ge0$, while the allowed reduction would give

$$
0\le-\frac12\bigl(2G(1/4)+G(3/4)\bigr).
$$

Both costs must be zero: their positive-weighted sum is nonnegative,
and the reduction forces it to be nonpositive. This is a necessary
condition under the temporary minimiser assumption, not a claim that
the two-weight candidate attains the minimum.

For a general minimiser, the same argument replaces the finite sum by
an integral. The direction $\eta=-\gamma$
is integrable, and $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$ remains admissible for
$0\le\varepsilon\le1$. It scales all existing mass by the same
factor. For the continuous candidate in Figure 1, it multiplies the
two nonzero slopes and the plateau height by $1-\varepsilon$;
it works for diffuse mass as well as atoms.
The weighted-sum identity becomes

$$
0\le D\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma]
=-\frac12\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu_\gamma(ds).
$$

The exchange of integration order is valid even if the total mass is
infinite. Its absolute integral is bounded by the area from Section 2:

$$
\int_{[0,1)}\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu_\gamma(ds)
=\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt
\le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty.
$$

Since $G\ge0$, its integral must be zero. If $G$ were positive at a
support point, continuity would bound it below by a positive number
on a neighbourhood carrying positive mass, contradicting that zero
integral. Hence $G=0$ on the support. This is **contact**: the
nonnegative function touches zero there. The scaling argument is the
variational argument of [Chen, Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen-support],
applied with the integrable-direction formula above.

Scaling removes only mass that exists. In Figure 1, even the supported
point $1/4$ has no atom: intervals around it carry mass, but the point
itself does not. Subtracting $\varepsilon\delta_{1/4}$ would create a
downward jump. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ the cumulative values would
remain nonnegative, but the function would no longer be nondecreasing.
Support alone does not permit atom removal. We have proved contact
on the support, not that every zero of $G$ must carry mass.

### 5.2 Contact gives endpoint conditions

We need information about $q$ at the ends of a possible gap. An interior
support point $s$ is a minimum of $G$. Since
$G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$, ordinary calculus gives

$$
q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1.
$$

At zero, if it belongs to the support, contact and symmetry give
$G(0)=q(0)=0$. If $q'(0)>1$, continuity would give $q'(t)>1$
for small positive $t$. Integration would then give $q(t)>t$, so
$G'(t)=t-q(t)<0$. Starting from $G(0)=0$, this would force $G(t)<0$,
a contradiction. Hence $q'(0)\le1$. This one-sided argument includes
an atom at zero.

### 5.3 Strict curvature creates an impossible integral

The support is relatively closed in $[0,1)$. Starting at a missing
point, enlarge its mass-free interval until it reaches support or a
boundary of the domain. Such a maximal interval has two
support endpoints, starts at zero outside the support, or reaches one.
We treat these three cases in order; the last includes empty support.

First suppose $(r,s)$ has both endpoints in the support, with
$0\le r<s<1$. Its constant height $c$ is necessarily positive:
for $t$ inside the gap, a small relative neighbourhood of $r$ lies in
$[0,t]$ and has positive mass, so $c=\mu_\gamma([0,t])>0$.
If $r=0$, this mass is an atom at zero. Contact imposes

$$
q(r)=r,\quad q(s)=s,\quad q'(r)\le1,\quad q'(s)\le1.
$$

The first two conditions require area $s-r$ under $q'$ across the gap.
A calculus model shows how strict convexity can prevent this. On the
earlier interval $[1/3,2/3]$, put $x=3t-1$ and consider the slope
$1-x(1-x)$. Its endpoints equal one, but

$$
\int_{1/3}^{2/3}[1-(3t-1)(2-3t)]\,dt
=\frac13\int_0^1[1-x(1-x)]\,dx=\frac5{18}.
$$

The missing area is $1/3-5/18=1/18$. This is a calculus model, not a
computed SK moment curve. The next input forces the actual $q'$ below
its endpoint chord in the same way.

**Strict-curvature input ([OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][support-curvature]).**
For any admissible coefficient equal to $c>0$ on an open interval,
its moment curve satisfies, strictly inside that interval,

$$
q'''(t)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

Section 7.3 explains how this sign is obtained after expectation.
The gap argument uses its strict sign; it does not use the particular
number $1/1000$.
The final inequality uses $a(t,x)>0$, proved by Gaussian smoothing
on the constant interval ([OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][support-regularity]);
convexity of $\Phi$ alone would only give $a\ge0$.
Because $q'''=(q')''$, the function $q'$ is strictly convex: between
two points its graph lies strictly below their joining chord.
The moment identity makes $q'$ continuous at the endpoints, even if
$\gamma$ jumps there; higher derivatives are needed only inside the gap.
Hence

$$
q'(t)<\frac{s-t}{s-r}q'(r)+\frac{t-r}{s-r}q'(s)\le1
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

At the step-coefficient, smooth-terminal stage, write $R_c=d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4$. The source constructs a correction $C$ from the spatial derivatives and the density factors, with $$ \mathbb E[C(t,X_t)]=0,\qquad R_c(t,x)+C(t,x)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}a(t,x)^4. $$ A rational polynomial identity gives the second inequality by writing the remainder as a sum of nonnegative terms. The density bounds and vanishing boundary products justify the first. Consequently $$ q'''(t)=\mathbb E[R_c(t,X_t)] =\mathbb E[(R_c+C)(t,X_t)] \ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ This is how the correction produces a useful lower bound for the expectation even though $R_c$ can be negative at particular states. To reach an arbitrary admissible coefficient, fix a time inside the plateau and approximate in $L^1$ by step coefficients, keeping the same value $c$ near that time. Uniform convergence of spatial derivatives through order four on a fixed strip below one, together with convergence of the coupled paths, passes the quantitative inequality to the limit. Strictness is then established for the limit itself: the constant-coefficient heat formula expresses $a$ as a nonnegative mean plus $c$ times a strictly positive variance of a nonconstant slope under a positively weighted Gaussian law. Hence $a(t,x)>0$ and its fourth moment is positive. Positivity of the approximants alone would not suffice. The auxiliary logarithmic derivatives need not converge: they have already been removed by integration. The analytic details are [OpenAI (2026a), §§3–5][support-manuscript] and the companion *Long Reasoning Record*, [§4.4, “How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful”](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-algebra), and [§4.5, “A fixed-time inequality and its plateau application”](../long/reasoning-record.md#plateau-limit).
